title: Johnny Dodds's clarinet, plus George Thomas, piano rolls and Jimmy Noone
summary: Dodds discusses Johnny's clarinets, reeds, embouchure, teachers and tooth loss, then George W. Thomas, piano rolls, Jimmy Noone, and Oliver's horns.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Now I can see what a good guy he was. What type of band do you think he enjoyed working in most? The bigger band or the smaller groups? He worked so many smaller groups. Was that by choice or was it just because they usually only hired three or four? That's all they were hired. Because he knew he could get as much out of the three or four men and he couldn't win five or six. He couldn't get the harmony, but there was work the man got. That's why we got the band of the Hot Seven. And that band put out the work of a band with twelve men. It was the seven. And like the band, he and Louis had the band of five. That Hot Five band put out as much music as ten men would put out. Well, if the man would put somebody else, he wasn't doing anything. He might have somebody that's working and have somebody that's not working. Somebody coming up from him. He was working. Do you remember anything about Johnny's clarinet? What kind he used? Well, I can't know. It was an Albert system, I understand. Do you remember they have what they call improved Albert sometimes? Well, he didn't use improved. An ordinary Albert. The old one, yes. I know that. I know that. Because he and Benny, Benny, Bonnie Bigard talked about that. Because Bonnie used the same kind he did. And then through, through the time change, Bonnie got the new kind and John didn't. And they often talked about it. Do you remember if he ever owned an A clarinet too? Oh yes. That's a B flat. Oh yes, he owned the two of them. He owned the two of them. A and B. Do you remember what kind of reeds he used? Whether they were hard reeds or soft reeds? He used the, I would say the hard reeds. Because the average person couldn't blow his clarinet. He and Bishis used hard reeds. They could blow each other's arms. They would even take it to burn the reed down. Make it stiff. You burn it down to make it stiffen? What did you do? Put a penny over it or a nickel or something like that? Yeah, well that's when they want to burn it off. It got too thin or too soft. They burn that part off. I was seeing them do that many days. Well, they'd take a half a dollar to do it. A half a dollar to get that curve. That's what they'd take. Yeah. Dime couldn't do it, nickel couldn't do it, and a quarter couldn't do it. It had to be a half a dollar. And I don't know, he was a peculiar fellow. He never would make anything tough for anybody. Only when he felt very mean, he'd make it tough for you. He'd get a piece of music and if you didn't like it, well that's a piece of music he's going to play. If it's tough for you, he'd say, well, he's joking, but I didn't send it for you, I sent it for your brother, what you coming with? Who wants to play a piece of music? That kind of a guy. He didn't mean it, but it made things wonderful. But you had to work. You weren't going to skate by or nothing. Oh, one other thing about Johnny and his, they have what they call the double embouchure. Some people put their upper teeth on the clarinet and the lower over, and others put the upper lip on top of their, under their teeth there too. Now wait a minute. Do you remember what she did? That's called the double embouchure. When you put both lips, none of your teeth touch. Or do you think he bit on to the upper part? No, he used his lips. That's why his music doesn't sound so much like staccato. He lifted, he lifted, everything he played he lifted. And he had to cut strong lips too. You think he covered his upper teeth too? The whole mouth. He put on his lips, his lips, done it. All the vibrato was through his lips. Both lips touched rather, you think, rather than the teeth, upper teeth. Now if he did lift teeth, I don't know. How did his teeth, that would be one thing most clarinetists that touch the teeth, their teeth wear. They're like George Lewis's teeth, they're all worn down. Well John didn't wear. He didn't have bad teeth there. Did he have his own teeth until he had them pulled when he was almost sick there at the end, you know? Yes, I think. He had them pulled. For a fact, I think he had them all pulled. The doctor, the doctor suggested that. Until that time he had his own teeth. His own teeth. But the thing about it, I see, now this is very peculiar. I saw the time when John had to have all his teeth extracted and he paid to play. And I saw John Lewis did the same thing. And they both asked the same question to me. It don't sound the same. I said, sure, it sounds fine. And they both had the same number to play. High Society. I think I told you about that, didn't I? No. You didn't mention once those last records that Johnny made were without the teeth. Yeah, it was in 1940. You did say that, yeah. To Decca. And then, this was in, in 40, 45, I made these with Lewis. 45. Yeah. I made those last records with Johnny in 40. And I made these with George Lewis in 45. He didn't have any teeth. So I've experienced men playing kind of without teeth. Same experience. And the both practically asked the same question. Yeah. Well, tell me more, a little bit more about George W. Thomas, if you can remember. What kind of style of piano did he play? Now I tell you. That's a long time ago. I remember that's been in the 14s. That's a long time. Yeah. 40. And here's the point about that. To have the touch and the tone and the way he played for that long time, I can't remember that. You don't remember if he played, well, say something like Jolly Roll Martin or did he play more blues or more ragtime or? Well, he didn't play, I'll say, just blues. He didn't do that. He played all numbers. The, the, the pop number was the same as any other, the George. Yep. Cause he was an entertainer. Did he sing too? Yeah, he sang. And he sang, he was actually a house entertainer. So you know about that he played no blues alone. And I worked with him those years. I just forgot just how it sounds. That was over 40 years ago. Nobody remember that part of it. And I've heard some men write and play on players. Some men write and this and some write and that. I just don't remember that part. Yeah. For a piano player, yes. I wouldn't say it for a band man. I just, I just done forgot. Yeah. But he wasn't real bad or anything like that. No, no, no. He used to read music. I know he composed quite a few pieces. Yeah. So you know, he knew he wasn't a bad guy. Yeah. But sometimes a composer's a good composer, but he can't execute much, you know. Well, he could. He could. He could. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He couldn't play. His wife was a better player than him, I thought. She was very tall too. Yes, I knew him. And she could play a lot of piano. But Richard was one of these kind of fellows that if you didn't know anybody, he'd put something over you. He used to play so and so and so and he never played before in his life. And when you get to play, then you know he didn't play nothing. And he was one of those kind of guys. And they got a whole lot of people like that. They could do this or that and can't do anything. Or he was one of those kind. Or I played that and such and such time. So that didn't get to play and then you'll find he didn't play nothing. You know that. But he was a good player. But you know what I like? Well I guess because I'm from the old school. I actually liked the piano rolls. You know those guys that had something in piano rolls, what you doing here today? That's right, I like them too. And it's just music. Wasn't that that it was doing so much, but it's the way it sounds. I like it myself. I do too. Like it all today. And you know what person, it's kind of wrapped up in music now, I'll send them to that. But she came playing Kay Thompson. She'd be a wonderful musician. At least she did. I sat around about 47, 48, Kay would have been a good musician. Oh did you ever play with piano rolls with your drums? I know in the theater when I was a kid in the picture show they had to play your piano and then they had a colored drummer come there, Doss Taylor they called him. He's dead now, come and play his drums at the piano. No, I never did like that because I know it was false. And I want nothing to do with nothing false. I want it to be a reality or nothing. Yeah, and yet you like to hear the piano rolls. Well not particularly. I like to hear the roll, but not put these drums onto it. Yeah, I know. But I know that was false. Yeah, that's right. I know. Now isn't that peculiar? Yeah. A lot of people just want to hear it anyway. No. I didn't want to hear anything false. I didn't want to hear anything put up. When I was coming along they had these uh, these pianists, upright pianists, to play for theaters. Had the drums and everything onto it. You remember those old pianists? Yeah. Well, people, I see people thought, oh this is the drummer. I just couldn't stand it. Because I know it was false. And I could hear a piece of the violin and everything. It didn't belong to me. Next thing. I was versatile in, in uh, in hearing things. If it wasn't, didn't fit, I would tell you, that don't fit me, man. Yeah. Now a lot of people can't do that. And uh, that's what made me so versatile in drumming. If I would do something myself and it didn't fit right or it didn't fit like I think it should or don't sound good, I wouldn't put it anymore. I wouldn't do it anymore. And of course I got a lot of things in my head to do for drumming. I don't know if I'm versatile enough for it. Now, uh, I'll tell you another thing that you've done for me and I'll thank you for it. I really thank you for it again and again and again. Uh, where you got those tom-toms pulled on those heads. Oh yeah, you like that? Very much, but I haven't been able to use it. Because at that time I was the first. I had no hands and uh, my, my coordination was off so that I couldn't do my hands like I wanted to. Well, I always did say I was going to do it, but I never did go into it. That's why I don't, that's why I don't play uh, uh, type today. You know, my hands was off. Well, um, before our tape is over, could you talk a couple of minutes or so about Jimmy Noon? If you can think of anything about him that might be of interest since he's not here either to tell us. Well, there's not too much I can tell about Jimmy. Jimmy was a quiet one. Oh, he's a quiet one. And you, you didn't know when you were doing good to when you wasn't with Jimmy. He didn't talk much. But, uh, you know anytime he hired you, what's be good for him. He was a good drummer. Or else he don't hire you. He was none of the Johnny Dodds. You're not good for me, I'm not gonna hire. I'm not gonna give you no chance to ruin nobody else. That's where he was. And Jimmy was a nice guy. I actually liked Jimmy. I liked to work for him. And anything you could do, Jimmy would let you do it. Anything you could throw in to make the band sound good or do suit yourself or bring something in that, that's bring you up, you could do it. He never tried to stop from doing anything you could do. Never did. And, uh, believe it or not, I was to go to California with Jimmy. I don't know if you knew that. When was that? In the late years? When he, when he went there. About 1941 or two or something? I know it's been 40. Oh, 40. 1041? Or 40. 1940, I think it was. Brother John died. Now he wanted me to go to California with him. Well, I'm glad I didn't go because that's where he died. Yeah. And I think he died in that same period when he went there. In 1944, I think he died. It was in 1944, well, and I would go time after. Maybe 43 along in there. Yeah. But I'm glad I didn't go because that was going to hit me terrible. It hit me terrible. Yeah, good. Because this had lost John in 40, when I was brand new yet. But that's a lot to work with Jimmy. Well, um, to get back to Johnny, did you ever hear him talk about who his favorite clarinetists were? Yeah. Who did he admire more than anyone? He admired Charlie McCurdy. That was his teacher. That was his teacher. And he loved him. He loved the man more than he didn't. He didn't even like George Barcai much to say Charlie. And, uh, for fact to me, or everybody else that time, he said, left the year, George Barcai played on Charlie. Yeah, he had a big following. But John rather than Charlie. He said, let's see, I think Charlie had a bigger tone than George, too. I think he did. Though his tone was very big for John. I never got to hear him. He never made records. Well, he was a deep tone man. Yeah. For fact, he used to play, he used to play so heavy, he sounded like a bass climber. Really? George, George was something like, I think that's who learned about where he learned from. Big Al-Lower. He said what Big Al-Lower learned from, sea climber. Sea climber. Sea climber. And Johnny never did play a sea, he played a and B. And I think George used to play, George used to play a B, A and B, too. I think McCurdy worked for A and B, but somehow, I know Johnny likes his tone. Mm-hmm. I don't know why. Um, anything about the trumpet players that Johnny used to, which, who was his favorite trumpet player, did he ever say? He worked with a lot of them, Oliver and Louie, and a lot of them in New Orleans, I guess. Did he talk about trumpet players much? No, he, he was the man to, of course he would give you something that you earned, and you had to earn it too. He, you know, and everything that John gives you. He didn't earn it, he wouldn't give it to you. But he used to like Louie, Louie was practice favorite. And, uh, Joe Oliver, well, he figured that Joe, Joe Oliver was the daddy, regardless. Yes. As Joe did wrong, and still Joe Oliver did that. And, uh, he was a man that, he'd give you what belongs to him, but you had to work for it. Better you got nothing from nothing from John. Yeah. John ain't gonna give you nothing for skating or, or pushing over this, pushing over, no sir, you had to work for it. Anytime you got something from John and John gives you the place for it, you worked for it, but you earned it. You get nothing from him. And I'm glad that he was that sort of a little brother to me. Yeah. Because I would, those days I'd go over it. I wouldn't care what, what I did, but he was, I just come right back over there. I ain't gonna let you do that. You gonna do it like anybody else. All right, John. Well, now that's what I want you to do. Do so and so and so. Well, John, I can do it like this. No, you know that's wrong. You know it's wrong yourself. That's why I do it. You better do it right, don't you? And, and, uh, uh, let's call it the same way. Uh, jello roll. No skeet, no jello roll. You done right or else you get down. Yeah. That's where John was. Did John ever have much trouble with the reeds and, I never heard him make a squeak or anything like that. Did he ever have much trouble? If he did, it was so seldom, that there wasn't notes anymore. Never even thought. What about Oliver? Did he ever miss many notes or was he a pretty perfect player? How did he? He's another guy. If he missed it, he blowed it out and you didn't know he missed it. Mm-hmm. He had power. Oh, power. That man could blow a note. He could take any horn brand new and blow it false. Blow it so hard and knock it out of tune. Knock it out of tune. Try like a piece of tin. I seen him do it. Uh, you know where he used to get his horns? He was, well, at Tom Browns. You know where Tom Browns was? He used to be on Lake Street. Oh, up here. Uh, no, west. No, I don't remember that. Well, he, I don't know how Joe found him, but in any way, he found him. Remember what makes he used most of the time? He used to use a york and he used to use, now first he used to use a Holton. He went from Holton to the York. In fact, I think that was the last one of the yorks. Do you remember any make with Johnny's clarinet? Did you get them from, were they French ones or? Yeah, all his, all his songs was French. I guess I imagine Buffet, most of them used Buffet. I don't know. Sometimes Selmer were coming out. No, he had Selmer too. He used Selmer a long, long time. He did? Well, that's a French man. Where did he buy his horns? Did he pick them up secondhand around here sometime? Or get them new? No, he would get them brand new. Because now they don't make them. You have to look around in secondhand stores to find it, Albert, you know. I guess those days you could buy them in a new store. Yeah, it was new. But he had an old one that he, his wife put up with a rubber thing and sitting in the machine. He had an old one that he wouldn't give nothing for. Put the rubber on it and rubber this and rubber that. Who had it? Johnny? Johnny. Yeah. He had to get rid of it, but he eventually had to get rid of it because it wasn't doing no good. Yeah. And after one winter it cracked and it came to leak it while then it would kill him. Yeah. And he had to get rid of it. And Sidney just happened so bad that he had to put one part in his pocket and go around and hold it until he got the other part. And he could play it, regardless of how regular it was. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well, what is he doing now? Is he playing now? Still in Paris, I guess. Oh, he's back there again. Oh, he's been there all the time. Oh, he's come back to New York and stay there quite a while. He was there for a while, but I think he's been there for a couple of years. That was the time when he had the Cadillac. I don't know. Oh, yeah. Well, you know how long that's been. That's been. Our tape is just about over. Unless there's something else you can think of about Johnny, you think he'd once said or it's... Well, nothing else right now. I think that covers it pretty good, maybe. And that was a great band, wasn't it? All those fellas in all of them, everyone a star. Every guy could work. Every guy was worth something. Every guy was at the back. And every guy giving his part, he's gone. And he didn't make no mistakes. None of them. That's why I would have to be some person. I'm nothing now, Bill, unless I had somebody of that caliber. I had somebody of that caliber, I could have them help to work. I could have them to work. Yeah. But without that, I can't work myself. Mm-hm.
